newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour, Conservatives trade food tax charges.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour, Conservatives trade food tax charges.

text.p: Britain's Labour party and Prime Minister John Major's ruling Conservatives traded bitter accusations over their tax plans on Thursday in a battle to win over voters before the imminent election.
Labour accused the government of planning to extend Value Added Tax to food, currently exempt.
The ruling party immediately hit back, denying any such plans and accusing Labour of negative campaigning in the run-up to an election due no later than May 22.
Labour, sure that VAT on food would be a highly unpopular with voters, stuck to its guns.

It said the Conservatives had gone back on tax promises after winning the 1992 election and had failed to give any details so far of what they would do if they won an unprecedented fifth consecutive term in office.
"There is a clear pattern," senior Labour Treasury spokesman Alistair Darling told a news conference.
"When the Tories (Conservatives) are asked if they have any plans to increase VAT, they deny it. When asked again, the Tories claim it is a smear. And once elected they increase VAT."

Quoting from speeches by Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke saying extending VAT to food was an option and that the ruling party wanted to extend the VAT base, Darling said: "The Tories simply cannot be trusted."
"VAT is the Tories favourite tax. Last time fuel. Next time food... There is no promise they won't break."

But Clarke denied any plans to entend VAT to food, saying the idea had never crossed his mind. "I have been four years as Chancellor. It has never crossed my mind to put VAT on food, and it hasn't crossed my mind now," he told a radio interviewer.
"I have never contemplated VAT on food. I am not contemplating VAT on food."
Conservative Party headquarters put out a news release accusing Labour of making up "fake Tory tax plans" and of failing to have detailed policies.

"Today they launch their third national negative campaign... Yet (Labour leader Tony) Blair and his colleagues have repeatedly denied that they would engage in negative campaigning. They say one thing, but they do another," it said.
Labour's attack is designed to neutralise Conservative charges that a Labour government would raise taxes, charges which opposition strategists believe cost it the last election.
Polls show Labour, which has a lead of some 20 points, is getting through to voters with its tax message.
The Conservatives have been hit by Labour's homing-in on the government's decision to raise VAT on fuel despite denials by Major before the 1992 election that he had any such plans.
Labour hammered home their message on Thursday with an election poster showing a hand breaking an egg, and the slogan "The next Tory tax? 10.50 a week on food. Enough is enough."

With little difference on policies between the two main parties, the campaign is being dominated by accusations and counter-accusations. With at most four months to go to the election, the campaign is getting more bitter by the day.
